108.t: Winning a raise from Hampton and Joe Glaser
108.s: Earning eleven dollars a night with Hampton, Wilder was sent to Gladys Hampton and manager Joe Glaser, told Glaser off, and got fifteen dollars.

108.s: Theater shows beyond union scale; Millinder tries to avoid paying extras and scolds Wilder for telling the others.
108.q: He was okay. As a leader he was all right, except that you had to watch him with the money. He’d get paid, and he was always pulling stunts. 242.s: Desvigne would cut each man's pay, explained through the 'see for yourself' saying; Brunious also mentions Herbert Leary's band.
242.q: Yeah, well, I know one thing, Sidney used to cut you a lot, too, man. You see, at that time, man, Jobs used to pay $3. You know? And, uh, well, each man in the band used to get $3, man, sure. 291.t: Who paid off the Oliver band
291.s: Asked who paid the band, Barnes says Oliver never did; Clarence Black, the director, handled it.
291.q: Joe Oliver never pays off himself. He always had someone who wanted to take that. Now, Clarence Black, when I first went out there, Clarence Black is the director. And he would do the paying off. He tend to have been.

198.t: Pay for managers and splitting job money fairly
198.s: Barnes says a manager should get only a dollar or two extra and he quit a band over a leader taking double.
198.q: But outside I'd rather pick a band. The same man doing things like, no, I want you. That's good. But a silly band, a bunch of man, you get together. 489.t: Getting paid: his own bands, Rollins and Turrentine
489.s: He sets pay in advance and pays his sidemen well; Rollins paid well, Turrentine did not, and nicknamed him The Squeeze.
489.q: Oh. Not getting paid is always not good. And I always keep that stuff in mind. Oh yeah. Definitely. And usually that’s done well in advance you know. So like I’ll know what I’m going to get paid and I know what everybody else is going to get, you know? So now I’m doing this gig at Small’s, I know…

382.t: The five-year contract, her salary and expenses
382.s: She earned about $750 at the club with weekly expenses withheld, and Claude had no business sense.
382.ch: From Pittsburgh to Maxine Sullivan: management and style
382.q: A five year contract. But, things began happening so fast, and as I said before, Claude couldn't do anything. He had gone as far as he could go. 147.t: Underpaid Sy Oliver and the Lunceford-Oxley ownership
147.s: Crawford says Sy resented his low pay and that Lunceford turned out to be a hired man whose road manager Dutch Williams handed him money.
147.ch: The Lunceford years: Europe, rivals and bandsmen
147.q: Because after all the time that I spent in that band, I used to see Dutch Williams, who was the road manager -- getting a little tired now, but I'm going to finish this. Come by every night after the job in the bus, and would give Lunceford some money.

18.t: Red Allen refuses him a raise at Cafe Society
18.s: Allen, as leader, told the owner not to give him $250, and said to pay what he said.
18.q: : They were paying $82 scale or something so I said, I'm not going to work for no scale. So I told Red, "You're the leader... I want your permission... to ask the owner for a raise [?] He said, "Higgy, how much money do you want?" I said, "$250 a week." He said, "O.K." And Red was standing behind…

74.t: Holder skims the band's raise and Mosley becomes manager
74.s: The hotel gives each man a $25 raise that Holder pockets until Trent asks; Mosley takes over as manager.
74.ch: Trent's band: Arkansas, Dallas and the Adolphus
74.q: He was a good man. He could play. Beautiful tone, and he could play. But he was a crook. That's how he lost his own band.
